title: Living in Harmony: What Health Actually Feels Like
reflection: Choose one set of precious minutes, such as the first twenty after waking, and fill it with one settling thing. What do you notice?

questions.q: How does Conversation 4.6 describe living in harmony, Ṛta?
o: A felt baseline of a system in tune, approached, lost and returned to across a life.
A peak of experience, held by sheer force once it has been reached through hard effort.
A rule of conduct, set out by teachers for all of those who wish to be good people.
A state of freedom from all difficulty, in which nothing is ever struggled with again.
questions.e: Ṛta is not enlightenment or an achievement held by force. It is the natural baseline of a system in tune. The hand-on-heart practice shows its signature: you do not command the heart, you breathe slowly and place attention, and the heart leans toward the breath on its own.
questions.c: Ṛta is a felt baseline, not a peak held by force

questions.q: At the end of a day a teacher notices that she is tired but not empty, and asks what gave her energy back. Which idea of Conversation 4.6 is she using?
o: Spent but not hollow: she is reading her own coherence from the inside, which is a useful signal.
A mind in Ṛta is never tired at all, so her tiredness shows that her practice has failed her.
A mind in Ṛta needs no rest at all, so she should hunt for what is wrong with her tiredness.
A mind in Ṛta forgets each day as it ends, so she should not look back over it at all.
questions.e: James’s practice is to notice at the end of each day: spent, or hollow? On spent-but-not-hollow days he looks back to find what gave the energy back. It is diagnostic and not prescriptive, and teaches him to read his own coherence from the inside.
questions.c: Spent but not hollow is a sign of coherence worth reading

questions.q: What is entrainment, according to Conversation 4.6?
o: The tuning of a thing to its own natural frequency, so that it draws energy from a field.
Coupled rhythms falling into step with no conductor, as the metronomes on a board do.
The slowing of every rhythm to a single speed, which is the speed of the breath.
The use of one strong rhythm to drown out all the weaker rhythms around it.
questions.e: Resonance is tuning to a natural frequency; entrainment is coupled rhythms synchronising, as five metronomes on a rocking board fall into unison, or breath and heart fall into step. Coherence is many rhythms in stable step, efficient because each part is held up by the others.
questions.c: Entrainment is coupled rhythms falling into step on their own

questions.q: “A healthy heart beats at a flat, steady rate, and health means as little variation as possible.”
questions.e: Health is living variability around a steady centre: a healthy heart speeds and slows constantly, never a flat line. Breathing at about six breaths a minute locks heart, breath and blood-pressure reflex into one measurable coherent wave.
questions.c: Health is living variability around a steady centre, not a flat line

questions.q: A woman realises that her first twenty minutes each morning are filled with a jangling feed. Which step fits Conversation 4.6?
o: Guard those minutes and put one coherent thing in them: a slow breath or a quiet word.
Drop the feed for good and every other screen too, since all of them are harmful to a mind.
Fill the minutes with as much news as she can, so that nothing in the day catches her out.
Leave the minutes just as they are, since what a person tunes to makes little difference.
questions.e: Entrainment is neutral: you fall into step with whatever holds you. The mind is always tuning to something, so choosing the station for the minutes that set your tone is itself a practice. Protect one set of minutes from the most agitating thing, and fill it with something settling.
questions.c: Choose the station for the minutes that set your tone

questions.q: “The mind is always tuning to something, and tuning to something more fragmented drags a person downward.”
questions.e: Tune to something more coherent, a steady breath, a calm person, the day-night cycle, and you are drawn upward. Tune to something more fragmented, a frantic feed or a panicked crowd, and you are dragged downward. There is no neutral, so choosing what to resonate with is perhaps the most fundamental practice.
questions.c: There is no neutral: what you tune to lifts you or drains you

questions.q: A doctor sees a patient with disrupted sleep, a scattered mind and a strained marriage. What does Conversation 4.6 suggest?
o: Choose whichever technique the patient is most likely to enjoy doing, and begin from there.
Ask which dimension of fit is most disrupted, and restore it first with a matching tool.
Treat every dimension at the same time, using the largest possible number of techniques.
Avoid choosing between them, since all techniques are equal and any one of them will do.
questions.e: Breathwork, yoga, light therapy, mindfulness and social-rhythm work are partial discoveries of one principle. Each restores a different dimension of fit: body clock, breath and heart, attention, daily rhythm or connection. Choosing a practice is choosing which broken rhythm to re-tune first.
questions.c: Restore the most disrupted dimension of fit first

questions.q: A man wants to prove entrainment to himself instead of taking it on trust. What does Conversation 4.6 suggest?
o: Read about it in several books, and accept it if all of the writers happen to agree on it.
Watch the metronome video, or feel heart and breath under his hand, so the physics is his own.
Ask other people whether they have felt it, and go along with what the majority of them say.
Leave the matter aside altogether, since a feeling of this kind cannot be tested by anyone.
questions.e: Kai’s two-part experiment is to watch the metronomes fall into unison, or to feel the heart and breath under his hand again, and then to audit his own day: what he is tuned to, hour by hour, and which things leave him more coherent. His own state is the readout.
questions.c: Make the physics your own by watching it, then audit your stations

questions.q: “The Schumann resonance, the Earth’s hum near meditative brain rhythms, is firmly proven and is one of the main supports of the framework.”
questions.e: Swamiji holds the Schumann resonance as intriguing but unproven: an open question and not something the argument leans on. The firmer supports are heart-breath coherence, nested brain rhythms, heart cells beating in unison and the body clock.
questions.c: The Schumann resonance is an open question, not a support

questions.q: A nurse on permanent night shifts asks why her disrupted body clock matters beyond feeling tired. What does Conversation 4.6 say?
o: Light tunes every organ to day and night, so chronic clock disruption is a real risk to health.
Light matters little, since the body soon adjusts fully to any rota that a person keeps up.
Light matters more than sleep, so she can do without a good night if she gets enough sun.
Light is a matter of taste, so she should arrange her hours to suit what she prefers.
questions.e: The suprachiasmatic nucleus, reset each morning by light, tunes every organ to day and night. This is ṛtu, Ṛta in time; the lesson notes that the WHO lists chronic night-shift clock disruption as a probable carcinogen. It is one of the scales at which fittedness runs.
questions.c: Light tunes the body clock; chronic disruption is a real risk
